blocks.text: SOAX in 2026: what you get

SOAX is a residential and mobile specialist known for granular filtering. Its 2026 pricing replaced fixed GB bundles with plans (Sandbox, Builder, Team, Scale, Enterprise) that include credits, and the credit burn rate depends on the exit country's tier. That makes SOAX cheap for some geographies and expensive for low-volume US work. The network is large (155M residential, 33M mobile advertised) and supports protocols few competitors offer, including UDP and QUIC.

Strengths: Residential and mobile on one balance; UDP and QUIC support alongside SOCKS5; Large pool with city and ISP targeting on every plan; Cheap traffic for Tier 2 and Tier 3 countries. Weak spots: Credits expire after 60 days; US traffic is expensive on small plans; Datacenter and ISP proxies were discontinued.
Webshare in 2026: what you get

Webshare is the self-service favourite of solo developers. It gives away 10 shared datacenter proxies with 1 GB a month forever, sells paid datacenter lists from $2.99 for 100 proxies, and offers static ISP and rotating residential networks with a clean dashboard and good API. Its rotating residential pool is listed at 80M+ IPs in 195 countries, with sticky sessions from one minute to 24 hours. The main catch is that monthly bandwidth resets every 30 days and does not roll over.

Strengths: Permanent free datacenter plan for testing; Low, transparent residential pricing; Excellent dashboard and API; Sticky sessions up to 24 hours. Weak spots: Bandwidth resets monthly with no rollover; No mobile proxies; 500-request default concurrency limit.
Pricing: SOAX vs Webshare

SOAX bills prepaid credits. For US (Tier 1) traffic, the no-fee Sandbox plan costs $5/GB, Builder ($200/month) $3/GB, Team ($500/month) $2.20/GB, and Scale ($1,500/month) $1.50/GB; cheaper countries cost less (Tier 3 from $2/GB on Sandbox). Credits expire 60 days after purchase, and SOAX counts traffic in both directions.

Webshare's rotating residential plans cost $3.50 for 1 GB, $27.50 for 10 GB, $65 for 25 GB, $225 for 100 GB and $875 for 500 GB per month, falling to $1.40/GB at 3 TB. Yearly billing is about 30% cheaper but is paid upfront for a 360-day term. Unused bandwidth resets every 30 days.

For a 10 GB month, Webshare costs about $27.50 while SOAX costs about $50, so Webshare saves around 45%. For a 100 GB month, Webshare costs about $225 while SOAX costs about $300, so Webshare saves around 25%. Both SOAX and Webshare work on allowances that do not carry forward indefinitely, so size your plan to real monthly usage rather than buying ahead.
Pool size, coverage and targeting

SOAX has the bigger advertised network, 155M residential + 33M mobile residential IPs against 80M+ for Webshare, roughly 1.9 times larger. Advertised pool sizes are marketing figures counted over long periods; the number of IPs actually reachable in a given country at a given moment is far smaller for every provider, so treat these as a rough guide to depth rather than a guarantee. For coverage, SOAX lists 195 countries and Webshare lists 195. On targeting, SOAX offers country, region, city and ISP; ASN and ZIP on Scale plans, while Webshare offers country, plus state, city or ZIP (US) or ASN.
Protocols, sessions and setup

Both providers support SOCKS5 as well as HTTP(S), so either will plug into scrapers, anti-detect browsers and automation tools that expect a SOCKS endpoint. On sessions, SOAX offers rotating or sticky; mobile sessions up to 60 minutes, and Webshare offers rotating or sticky from 1 minute to 24 hours. Setup works the same way on both: a single gateway endpoint, with location and session options passed as username parameters, plus IP whitelisting if you prefer not to use credentials.
Which is better for your use case?

General web scraping: tie. Neither has a clear edge. With SOAX: a large pool and its own error headers help debugging. With Webshare: low prices and a developer-friendly API. Run the same small test on both before committing.
SERP and rank tracking: SOAX wins. The deciding factor for SOAX: city and ISP targeting for local results. The limitation on the Webshare side: fine for light rank tracking.

Social media and multi-account management: SOAX wins. The deciding factor for SOAX: mobile IPs on the same balance as residential. The limitation on the Webshare side: 24-hour sticky sessions and cheap static ISP IPs.
E-commerce price and stock monitoring: SOAX. SOAX has the edge here. Why: granular location filters. How Webshare compares: good for US work with ZIP targeting, thinner elsewhere.

Ad verification and geo-testing: SOAX wins. The deciding factor for SOAX: ISP, ASN and carrier-level targeting. The limitation on the Webshare side: no mobile network and limited selector combinations.

Tight budgets: Webshare wins. The deciding factor for Webshare: free tier plus some of the lowest per-GB rates here. The limitation on the SOAX side: cheap in Tier 3 countries but pricey for small US jobs.
Trials, verification and billing fine print

Before you pay, check how each provider lets you test. SOAX: Paid 3-day trial, 400 MB for $1.99. Webshare: 10 free datacenter proxies (1 GB/month); no residential trial. Verification and payment rules differ too. SOAX: Verification for postpaid and enterprise terms. Webshare: ID checks only when flagged or for restricted categories. Whichever you choose, measure cost per successful request rather than cost per gigabyte: retries, blocked pages and heavy page assets all burn bandwidth, and a cheaper network that fails more often can end up costing more. Blocking images and fonts in your scraper, reusing sessions where a target allows it, and capping concurrency are the quickest ways to cut the bill on either provider.
How to test SOAX and Webshare before you commit
Spec sheets only get you so far. A short, structured test on your own targets will settle SOAX vs Webshare faster than any review:
1. Buy the smallest option on each side (SOAX: paid 3-day trial, 400 MB for $1.99; Webshare: 10 free datacenter proxies (1 GB/month); no residential trial).
2. Pick three to five real target URLs and the two or three countries that matter most, and send the same number of requests (a few hundred is enough) through each provider at the same time of day.
3. Record success rate, median response time, CAPTCHAs or blocks, and the number of unique exit IPs you received per country.
4. Divide what you spent by the number of successful, correctly located responses to get cost per useful request, then scale that to your monthly volume.
Bottom line

Across the six use cases above, SOAX comes out ahead in 4, Webshare in 1, and 1 is a tie. That makes SOAX the safer default if you are unsure, but the right answer still depends on your volume and targets: SOAX is strongest for mobile-first work such as app testing and social platforms, while Webshare is strongest for solo developers and small teams. If you can, spend a few dollars testing both on the exact sites and countries you care about; a one-hour test tells you more than any spec sheet.
